strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: discovering and segmenting image categories without user-provided class names. Its modular approach can extend existing open-vocabulary segmentors without additional model training.

Decoding subsets of clustered BLIP patch embeddings is an interesting way to obtain local descriptions from an image-level captioning model. Reusing BLIP for both clustering and captioning provides a coherent alternative to pipelines that combine several representation spaces.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across three datasets: SELF-SEG improves class-agnostic mIoU over BLIP captions plus X-Decoder from 38.0 to 41.9 on VOC, 26.7 to 29.2 on ADE20K, and 29.2 to 35.8 on CityScapes.

The pipeline is clearly illustrated, reused models and datasets are attributed, and several implementation parameters and evaluator prompts are supplied. Appendix B usefully documents hallucinated labels, overly generic descriptions, and competition between related categories.
weaknesses: The principal concern is the validity of LOVE, on which SELF-SEG's semantic mIoU results depend. No human-checked mapping accuracy, comparison against the rejected embedding-based evaluators, or sensitivity analysis is reported. Appendix A instructs the LLM to map stuff terms to background even for ADE20K and CityScapes, which contain valid stuff categories; the exact-match override only partly mitigates this. ADE20K's 847-class vocabulary is not supplied to the LLM at all. These choices can materially affect scores and require validation.

Table 2 does not establish comparable evaluation and supervision for the central ZeroSeg comparison. SELF-SEG inherits X-Decoder's segmentation training, whereas the cited baseline targets zero segment labels, and the manuscript does not establish that ZeroSeg was reevaluated with LOVE. Thus, 41.6 versus 20.1 mIoU does not isolate improved self-guidance. The ADE20K and CityScapes state-of-the-art claims also lack competing automatic-class-generation results.

Evidence for the specific BCC design is incomplete. Table 1 uses oracle class-agnostic matching, which measures region coverage but cannot establish whether generated names are correct. Semantic evaluation of the plain-caption baseline, noun precision/recall, and comparisons with equal caption-generation budgets would better substantiate the contribution. The benefits of multi-scale clustering, alignment, and denoising are not individually demonstrated.

The evaluation protocol leaves possible selection bias unresolved. Section 4.1 describes Bayesian hyperparameter optimization on Pascal VOC without identifying a tuning split disjoint from evaluation. Table 3 supplies dataset-specific best captioning-cycle counts used in the headline results, again without a separate selection protocol. Repeated-run variability is also absent despite stochastic clustering and caption generation.

Some consequential implementation details remain ambiguous. Equation 10 describes independent maximum-IoU assignments rather than the globally constrained Hungarian matching named in the text. Alignment between the 24-by-24 and 32-by-32 grids is unspecified, as is whether the additional 256 positional dimensions are removed before passing embeddings to the fixed-width pretrained BLIP decoder.

Practical efficiency is uncharacterized: there are no runtime or memory measurements despite repeated captioning of multiple clusters, including 20 cycles for the reported CityScapes result. This limits assessment of the pipeline's deployment value.
